newsitem.title: USA: Consumer sentiment index ties all-time high - sources.
newsitem.headline: Consumer sentiment index ties all-time high - sources.

text.p: The University of Michigan's preliminary index of consumer sentiment for April tied the all-time high set in March 1984 at 101.0, market sources said Friday.
"At 101.0, the index matches its level of March 1984, the record for the series since it started on a monthly basis in 1978," a market source told Reuters.
The University of Michigan, which releases its index only to paying subscribers, declined any comment on the data.

Financial market sources reported earlier Friday the index rose to 101.0 in early April from 100.0 in March. The current conditions component surged to 116.7 from 109.8, while the expectations component slipped to 90.9 from 93.6.
"This is the first time the index registered back-to-back readings of 100 or higher. Record confidence implies the consumer will continue to fuel growth," the source added.

"This means a very small likelihood consumers will cut back on spending," said Conference Board economist Michael Boldin, who calculates the Leading Economic Indicators index, of which the Michigan expectations index is a component.
Another market source said, "It's only the fifth time since the index was created that it stands at or above 100."
The source said the index hit triple digits three times in 1984 and twice this year.
Boldin said the strength in the Michigan index "is consistent with everything we see. You can't see any number that tells you the American consumer is worried."

The Conference Board economist said the pullback in the expectations component was not an indication Americans were concerned about the future since "those numbers are high, anyway, optimistic at these levels."
Boldin added that consumers have good reasons to be upbeat about spending since jobs are plentiful, wages are rising faster than prices and inflation is fairly low.

"By every measure, the unemployment rate is as low as anybody would have expected. Wages are more than keeping up with inflation. There is nothing in the cards right now (indicating) this expansion is going to end," Boldin said.
The Conference Board economist also stressed job insecurity is a factor that has probably been "overplayed."
"And if job insecurity ever was that strong, it certainly is going out of the picture," he said.
David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities International, said the upbeat mood mirrored the extremely good economic conditions.

"Historically, if you look at the U.S. unemployment rate and inflation rate, you can pretty much know how Americans feel," said Resler who pointed out the jobless rate is at its lowest since 1989 and inflation at its lowest since 1964.

Resler noted the high level of consumer confidence did not reflect an economic rebound like in the 1980s, but "a growing recognition among Americans that we are enjoying almost unprecedented healthy conditions."
